summary: Summarizes deployment scenarios and operational experience with NAT64, which lets IPv6-only clients reach IPv4 servers. It considers both carrier-grade NAT64 and a NAT64 server front end.

eli5.summary: Some networks only speak the new address language. A translator lets them talk to old-language sites. This reports how people set up these translators and what they learned.

subtitle: How to deploy NAT64 translators connecting IPv6-only networks to the IPv4 Internet.

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks must eventually coexist with the IPv4 Internet. IPv6-only hosts need a way to reach IPv4-only servers, but NAT64 translation is complex to deploy and operate at scale.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents real-world NAT64 deployment patterns in two scenarios: carrier-grade NAT (NAT64-CGN) in ISP networks, and server front-end translation (NAT64-FE) in data centers. It covers high availability, logging, geolocation, and application compatibility.
tldr.outcome: Operators have tested NAT64 deployments and learned which services work, what breaks, and how to design for redundancy and scale.

today: RFC 7269 is an Informational RFC documenting operational experience with NAT64 deployment. It remains valid as NAT64-CGN continues to be deployed by mobile operators globally, and NAT64-FE remains relevant for data centers transitioning to IPv6.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are nearly exhausted, so new networks must operate as IPv6-only. However, IPv4 services will exist for years, so IPv6-only hosts need a way to reach them. NAT64 is a translation mechanism that converts between IPv6 and IPv4 on behalf of IPv6 clients.

The XMPP community and mobile operators have experimented with NAT64 for years. At least 30% of service providers plan to deploy some form of NAT64 and DNS64. This document captures operational experience from carriers and content providers to guide future deployments.
sections.eli5: The Internet is running out of old addresses, so new networks use the new addressing language. Translators let those networks talk to old services that only speak the old language.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
NAT64 can be deployed in two main topologies. NAT64-CGN (Carrier-Grade NAT) sits in an ISP or mobile operator's network, translating traffic from IPv6 subscribers to reach the IPv4 Internet. The operator controls the IPv6 side but has limited control over the external IPv4 services. NAT64-FE (Front End) sits in a data center or content provider's network, translating incoming IPv6 requests to internal IPv4 servers. The operator controls both sides but only sees IPv6 clients from outside.

DNS64 is essential: it synthesizes IPv6 addresses for IPv4-only services so clients know how to reach them through NAT64. Stateful NAT64 is better for maximizing sharing of limited IPv4 addresses, while stateless NAT64 provides better transparency when combined with address-sharing protocols.
sections.eli5: You can put the translator at the ISP (for all IPv6 customers to use) or at a data center (for customers to reach one service). The translator needs a DNS helper to tell clients where to send their requests.

sections.title: Operating NAT64 at Scale
sections.content:
High Availability is critical. Three redundancy modes are used: Cold Standby (manually switched, disconnects existing sessions), Warm Standby (automatic but sessions restart), and Hot Standby (automatic with session continuity). Hot Standby requires synchronizing session state between primary and backup, needing a 10 Gigabit transport link for scale. In testing, Hot Standby reduced failover time to 35 milliseconds for 30 million sessions.

Logging for traceability is expensive at scale. A NAT64-CGN serving 200,000 subscribers generates 42.5 terabytes of raw logs daily. Bulk port allocation reduces this to one thousandth of the volume, but decreases IPv4 address sharing efficiency. Operators must balance compliance, storage investment, and address utilization.

Geolocation breaks with NAT64 because all traffic from the operator appears from one address pool. ISPs can subdivide the IPv4 pool geographically, or use HTTP headers to pass the original IPv6 address. Data centers can integrate NAT64 with load balancers that understand client information.
sections.eli5: Running a translator at scale needs backup systems for when the main one fails. You also need to keep detailed logs for legal reasons, but that creates a huge data storage problem. And websites that guess where you are based on your IP address will think everyone in a region is in one place.

sections.title: Application Compatibility and Experience
sections.content:
Not all applications work through NAT64. Web services mostly work (about 43% of the top 100 websites are accessed through NAT64 because they are dual-stack), but instant messaging fails because clients cannot support IPv6. Games work if they are web-based but fail if they require IPv6 support in the application. FTP and email work; SIP voice calls fail without proper NAT traversal; IPsec VPN fails unless it uses NAT-traversal mode. P2P applications generally fail due to lack of IPv6 support in the software.

Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) can fix some protocols by translating embedded IP addresses in control messages, but ALGs reduce performance. A better solution is upgrading applications to use IPv6 natively, which avoids translation overhead and the risk of application failures.
sections.eli5: Websites work fine through the translator. Games and chat programs often don't because they were not designed for it. Voice calls need special tricks. The best answer is to update old software to use the new address language natively.

sections.title: Security and Other Issues
sections.content:
NAT64 deployments face several challenges beyond translation. IPv6 fragmentation behavior differs from IPv4, and small MTU links can trigger fragmentation problems. Configuring IPv4 MTUs above 1260 bytes can prevent this in data centers, but is hard to enforce on the open Internet.

Security mechanisms like DNSSEC conflict with DNS64 synthesis: DNSSEC validation fails when DNS64 modifies answers. Operators should monitor DDoS attacks on NAT64 devices and deploy rate limiting. Stateless NAT64 removes the DDoS state-management burden, while stateful NAT64 is at risk from connection floods.

Unique Local Addresses (ULAs) work poorly as NAT64 prefixes in dual-stack networks because hosts follow RFC 6724's preference rules and avoid ULAs, bypassing NAT64. Global Unicast Addresses are a better choice.
sections.eli5: Encryption systems designed to prevent message changes break when the translator modifies packets. Attackers can flood the translator with fake connections. Very old networks with tiny data packets sometimes have trouble, but new networks can be configured to avoid this.

left.title: NAT64-CGN
left.desc: Deployed in ISP or mobile network. Operator controls IPv6 side, limited control over IPv4.

right.title: NAT64-FE
right.desc: Deployed in data center as load balancer or firewall. Operator controls IPv4 internal network.
